headings.title: Introduction to Control Measures in Drug Administration
headings.content: Control measures in drug administration are systematic steps and checks designed to ensure medications reach the right patient safely and effectively. In busy Nigerian healthcare settings, from primary health centres to tertiary teaching hospitals, procedural shortcuts easily compromise patient safety. These measures act as barriers against preventable adverse drug events, hospital-acquired complications, and fatalities. Every nurse carries professional and legal responsibility for every drug handed to a patient. Therefore, strict adherence to institutional protocols and national drug policies remains mandatory at all times.

headings.title: The Rights of Medication Administration
headings.content:
Applying the **Rights of Medication Administration** forms the bedrock of safe nursing practice. Traditionally taught as five rights, modern clinical practice expands this framework to seven or more to address complex pharmacological environments.

- **Right Patient**: Verify identity using at least two unique identifiers before giving any drug.
- **Right Medication**: Compare the drug label against the prescription order three times.
- **Right Dose**: Calculate dosages carefully and double-check high-alert medications with a colleague.
- **Right Route**: Confirm the method of delivery matches the prescriber's exact instruction.
- **Right Time**: Administer drugs within the prescribed timeframe to maintain therapeutic blood levels.
- **Right Documentation**: Record the administration immediately after giving the drug, never beforehand.
- **Right Reason**: Understand the clinical indication for the prescribed drug in relation to the patient's condition.

headings.title: Pre-Administration Patient Assessment and Verification
headings.content: Before any medication touches a patient, targeted baseline assessments must occur. Nurses check vital signs, current laboratory results, and known allergies. For instance, administering an antihypertensive drug without checking current blood pressure risks precipitous hypotension. Asking open-ended questions about previous allergic reactions uncovers hidden sensitivities that charts might miss. Verification also involves checking if the patient's clinical status has changed since the doctor wrote the order, rendering the drug temporarily unsafe.

headings.title: Medication Reconciliation and Prescription Interpretation
headings.content: Unclear handwriting, ambiguous abbreviations, and incomplete medication histories cause dangerous clinical errors. **Medication reconciliation** is the formal process of comparing a patient's current home medications against newly admitted orders to avoid omissions, duplications, or dangerous drug interactions. Nurses must never guess an illegible prescription. When an order lacks a dose, route, or frequency, clarifying directly with the prescriber is mandatory. A common pitfall is assuming standard adult dosages without checking pediatric or geriatric adjustments.

headings.title: Standard Safety Checks and Calculations
headings.content:
Mathematical accuracy in drug calculation is a vital life-saving skill. Nurses perform the **three label checks**: first when retrieving the medication from storage, second when preparing or pouring the dose, and third at the bedside before administration. 

| Check Stage | Action Required | Location |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| First Check | Compare drug label with medication sheet | Medicine cupboard / Trolley |
| Second Check | Verify calculations and measure dose | Medication preparation area |
| Third Check | Confirm identity and label one last time | Patient bedside |

High-alert medications such as insulin, heparin, and opioids always require a second independent nurse calculation to eliminate human error.

headings.title: Aseptic Techniques and Environmental Controls
headings.content: Contamination during drug preparation introduces pathogens directly into the bloodstream or sterile body cavities, leading to sepsis. Nurses must practice strict **aseptic technique** when handling parenteral medications, IV lines, and wound-associated topicals. Work surfaces must be cleaned with appropriate antiseptic wipes before tray setup. Hand hygiene must be performed before and after touching any medication packaging. Never touch the needle, syringe hub, or the inner surface of sterile container caps during preparation.

headings.title: Post-Administration Monitoring and Documentation
headings.content: The nursing cycle does not end when a patient swallows a pill or receives an injection. Post-administration monitoring evaluates therapeutic efficacy and watches for unexpected adverse reactions. For instance, a patient receiving a narcotic analgesic requires respiratory rate checks within specific intervals. Documenting the exact time, route, and patient response completes the communication loop. Delayed documentation leaves oncoming shifts blind to what interventions have actually been completed.

headings.title: Reporting and Managing Medication Errors
headings.content: Despite rigorous safeguards, medication errors still occur due to fatigue, systemic failures, or communication breakdowns. When an error happens, immediate patient safety assessment takes precedence over disciplinary concerns. The nurse must stabilize the client, notify the attending physician, and monitor vital signs closely. Blame-free reporting cultures encourage open disclosure, allowing institutions to identify root causes and redesign workflows to prevent recurrence.
